I am finding so many different answers I'm having a hard time finding a definitive one on the internet.

~How many solar systems (Ones confirmed) are in our Milky Way Galaxy?

~How many Galaxies (Ones confirmed) are in our universe?

~Are there any other known universes in the cosmos?

Confirmed Solar Systems: We don't know. This number is increasing everyday. We are finding new planets beyond our own Solar System every week and as technology improves, we will only find more planets faster. If you consider a sun with a single planet around it, the number is in the thousands.

Galaxies in our Universe: The number is so big no one has bothered to count precisely. We can only estimate, but that estimate is in the trillions. If you want an exact number, you better go ahead and start counting.

Other Universes: What you are asking is entirely theoretical. If we found another Universe other than ours it would completely upend our understanding of how everything formed. We would have to develop entirely new models to explain this and so far our models hold up (mostly) to the one Universe theory.

Via Wikipedia: 1956 planets in 1239 planetary systems including 488 multiple planetary systems as of 12 September 2015.

I've interpreted the second question as "the number of named galaxies". http://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/CATALOGS/naga.html is the best I could find. This is a difficult one to find an answer for, as I've seen counts as high as nearly 30,000, yet no definitive lists greater than the one previously mentioned.

Your third question is a bit strange. Cosmos and universe are sometimes used interchangeably. The best answer I can give is that there are models of existence wherein multiple universes can exist (in some way or another). However, there have been no confirmed observations of another universe.

"...there may be tens of billions of solar systems in our galaxy, perhaps even as many as 100 billion."

"According to the best estimates of astronomers there are at least one hundred billion galaxies in the observable universe."

It sounds strange, but you need to define confirmed.

In science we can predict many things beyond a reasonable doubt that cannot be immediately 'seen'. Although that kind of begs one to ask what seeing even is. For instance Neptune's existence was predicted and it's location determined with incredibly accuracy before we could ever see it. But if we can see its gravitational effects and determine exactly where it is, its approximate size, and so forth is that so different than somebody observing light with a certain wavelength bounce off of it?

In any case the answer is going to be something like: a whole lot, a number that makes "a whole lot" look really really small, and asterisk. The last one being that directly observing another universe ought be impossible by how we define a universe, yet paradoxically there are an increasing number of hypothesis on how we may actually be able to indirectly observe and even test for the existence of other universes.
